title: A second text
hookLine: one from another tradition, kept apart: Thoreau bathed his mind in the Bhagavad Gita at Walden and called it by its own name
tomorrow: how did a whole library of teachings survive with no books at all?

cards: Winter at Walden Pond. Thoreau is watching ice cutters saw blocks out of his pond, to be shipped off to faraway ports, India among them. And he's been reading, mornings, a Hindu scripture.
He writes: "In the morning I bathe my intellect in the stupendous and cosmogonal philosophy of the Bhagvat Geeta."
Then he follows the ice in his mind across the ocean: "The pure Walden water is mingled with the sacred water of the Ganges."

teach.b: Here's the question: is it all right to read another tradition's holy book, and how? Thoreau's own picture is of waters mingling, and his reading did flow into his own writing.
But notice what he keeps doing: he names both. Walden water. The Ganges.
The Bhagvat Geeta, credited by title, never passed off as his. That's this path's rule: draw from any tradition, always by name. A second text, on another shelf.
Now the neighbor, in its own words.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that nothing in this world purifies like knowledge.
That's what's shared: Thoreau's morning bath for the mind, and the Gita's teaching that true knowledge makes a person clean. And one honest difference.

teach.h: KRISHNA'S WORD, OR A POND-SIDE BOOK.
teach.b: For Hindus, the Gita is Krishna's teaching, God speaking to Arjuna, recited in devotion, part of a living faith with temples, festivals and families.
Thoreau, by his own words, read it as philosophy, mornings, beside a pond. Same pages, very different shelves.
That's why you keep a second text apart: so it can stay what it is to the people who hold it sacred.
Read it with respect, learn from it, and never pretend the two books are one.

how: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita as Krishna's teaching. People on their own path who read across traditions can keep a second text from another tradition, read by its own name and with respect, apart from their main book.

games.q: a friend loves the Gita and wants to mix its verses into her own homemade prayer book. by this path's rule, what fits?
o: keep the Gita whole and named, on its own shelf, and read it with respect.
blend the best lines of every book into one, since they all mean the same.
avoid it entirely; a second tradition will only confuse the first.
games.why: Thoreau named the Gita and never claimed it as his. Keeping it apart lets it stay what it is to the people who hold it sacred.

practice: Stand, if you can, and walk slowly for about a minute, the way Thoreau walked down to his pond. As you walk, name your main book, and then one book from another tradition you'd like to learn from. Then sit, and let the walk settle.

wordCard.voice: A second text: one book from another tradition, read with respect and kept apart, by its own name, the way Thoreau kept the Gita.
